newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England committee starts with rate dilemma.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England committee starts with rate dilemma.

text.p: The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, begins its first two-day meeting later on Thursday amid unprecedented uncertainty over the outcome.

Interest rate futures contracts are factoring in a quarter-point rate rise but the radical changes made to Britain's monetary framework by the new government, coupled with mixed inflationary signals from economic data, mean few analysts are making forecasts with any confidence.
The monetary committee is faced with setting policy for an unbalanced economic recovery that displays a lively services sector but sluggish manufacturing output growth.

In addition, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown is set to clarify the bank's inflation target at next week's Mansion House speech, closely followed by his first budget on July 2. So the bank may choose to hold fire.

"The bank is probably itching to raise rates but the next month will bring the budget, news on the inflation target and evidence of the impact the windfall payments are having on consumption. So I think it may decide to hold off until July," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
A number of building societies are converting into banks this year, showering members with shares totalling 30 billion pounds ($49 billion) in the process.
The Halifax, Britain's largest mortgage lender, floated on Monday and issued shares worth more than 17 billion pounds.

The outcome of the meeting will be made public at 1100 GMT on Friday. A Reuter poll of 21 economists showed a narrow majority anticipated a rate increase, with 12 expecting base rates to rise to 6.5 percent from the present 6.25 percent.

The major economic risk in raising rates lies with the exchange rate. Britain's manufacturing sector has been ravaged by the pound's recent strength -- up almost 20 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August -- and is growing only slowly.
Meanwhile, the bigger services sector, insulated from the exchange rate by its largely domestic customer base, is booming.
A rate rise on Friday could send the pound even higher, hitting the weakest part of the economy hardest.

The bank has tended to downplay the impact of the pound's rally on the economy but on Wednesday Governor Eddie George surprised markets by saying the exchange rate would be the key focus at the meeting.

"The immediate problem is to balance the degree of tension between the pressure of domestic demand, which has been running a bit above a sustainable rate, with the exaggerated strength of the exchange rate," he told reporters in Switzerland.
Robert Barrie, UK economist at BZW, said this fresh enthusiasm about the effect on the pound could suggest a rate rise is less likely on Friday.
"The bank has acknowledged that sterling is complicating matters and that is slightly reassuring for those who don't want to see rates going up," he said.

Those forecasting a rate rise are relying heavily on the contents of the Bank of England's last inflation report. The newly-empowered central bank made clear in the report that monetary policy is too loose if underlying inflation is to hit the government's existing 2.5 percent target.
In addition to the economic dilemma, uncertainty comes from the structure of the new committee.
Six members will attend the first meeting with full voting rights, with bank insiders comfortably outnumbering outsiders.
The Bank of England officials are George, deputy governor Howard Davies and executive directors Mervyn King and Ian Plenderleith.

The two outside appointees attending are Charles Goodhart, Professor of Banking and Finance at the London School of Economics, and Willem Buiter, Professor of International Macroeconmics at Cambridge University.

A third outside committee member, Sir Alan Budd, chief economic adviser to the Treasury, will be at the meeting as the non-voting Treasury observer. He will take up his voting position on the committee when he retires from the Treasury later this year.
DeAnne Julius, British Airways Plc chief economist and the last outside appointee, will join the committee in September.

"No one really knows what message this committee will want to send," said Barrie. "But while they will want to be tough on inflation, they will not want to look as though they are being panicked into a decision at their first ever meeting."
